opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that robotics has always had a data problem disguised as an algorithm problem. For a long time, every lab built its own robot, collected its own small dataset for one task in one environment, and trained a model that worked only there. You'd get a nice demo, but nothing compounded. The essential question was never "can we make one robot fold one towel?" It was "how do we get a system that keeps getting better as it sees more of the world?"

The partner approach goes straight at that. Instead of us trying to own every robot, every deployment, and every environment, we work with partners who have real hardware in real settings: homes, warehouses, factories, different embodiments, different tasks. That gives us diversity we could never manufacture in our own building. Diversity is what generalization comes from. If a model only ever sees our lab's lighting, tables, and objects, it learns our lab. If it sees hundreds of messy real-world settings, it starts to learn something closer to physical common sense.

The second piece is the feedback loop. A partner deploying a model hits failures we'd never think to test for. Those failures are the most valuable data. They tell you where the model's understanding breaks down. So the partnership isn't just distribution, it's how the foundation model learns what it doesn't know.

And third, it reflects a bet about where value sits. We think the hard, shared part is the general-purpose brain, something like a foundation model for the physical world. The hardware, the specific application, the customer relationship: other people can do those better and in more places than we can. If the model is good enough, it should be useful across all of them. Partnering lets us focus on the piece we think is essential, and lets the whole ecosystem scale faster than any single company could alone.

So to me it's less a business strategy than a research strategy. It's how you get the scale and variety of real-world experience that intelligence in the physical world actually requires.

r001.rationale: The response says Pi works with partners deploying models on real hardware in varied settings, and that deployment failures provide valuable data for the model’s learning. It frames this as a research strategy for improving the foundation model.

r002.rationale: The response describes a general-purpose model intended to be useful across different hardware and applications, but does not say that plugging it into newly assembled robot hardware would give that hardware many capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look at what Pi is doing with the partner model, I think it's honest about where the field actually is. Everyone wants to talk about a general-purpose robot foundation model, but the uncomfortable truth is that the bottleneck isn't the architecture, it's data. Vision and language got to scale because the internet handed them trillions of tokens for free. Robotics has no internet. Every useful trajectory has to be generated by a physical arm touching a physical object in a real environment, and that is slow, expensive, and messy.

So the question becomes: who has the robots, who has the environments, and who has the tasks that matter? Pi decided they shouldn't try to own all of that themselves. Instead of building one factory or one warehouse and overfitting to it, they go to partners who already have real deployments, real failure modes, and real economic pressure. The partner gets a model that actually works on their hardware, and Pi gets diversity, which is the single most important ingredient for generalization. A policy trained on one kitchen learns that kitchen. A policy trained across fifty partners' kitchens, warehouses, and labs starts to learn something about kitchens in general.

The second thing I'd point to is that the partner approach forces the research to confront the deployment gap early. In academia you can publish a ninety percent success rate on a benchmark and move on. A partner running a line doesn't care about your benchmark. They care about the ten percent, and they'll tell you exactly how it fails at three in the morning. That feedback loop is painful, but it's where the essential questions live: how do you handle distribution shift, how do you recover from mistakes, how do you get the robot to ask for help instead of knocking over the shelf.

And then there's the hardware question. Nobody knows what the right embodiment is yet. Humanoids, mobile manipulators, fixed arms. By working across partners with different platforms, Pi is implicitly betting that the model should be embodiment-agnostic, and they're collecting the evidence to find out whether that bet holds. If one brain can drive many bodies, the economics of the whole industry change.

So to me it's less a business strategy and more an admission about the nature of the problem. Robotics is going to be solved in the world, not in a lab, and the partner model is a way to live in the world while you're still doing the research.

r001.rationale: It describes partnering with organizations that have real deployments and economic pressure, giving Pi varied data and real-world feedback that advance research on generalization and deployment failures.

r002.rationale: It suggests one embodiment-agnostic model might drive different robot bodies, but does not say that newly assembled hardware can gain many capabilities by plugging in a reusable model component.

astra-6.text:
I think the Partner approach gets at a fundamental question: how does a robot become useful alongside people? It’s one thing to complete a task in isolation. It’s another to understand what someone wants, adapt when circumstances change, and recognize when to ask for help.

Looking at the robot as a partner brings those challenges together. Capability matters, but so do communication, reliability, and human judgment. To me, that’s why this approach is meaningful: it puts the relationship between people and robots at the center of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots working alongside people, but does not mention collaborating with companies that commercially deploy robots or advancing Pi’s research frontier indirectly.

r002.rationale: The response says capability matters, but does not describe Pi’s general model as a reusable component that gives newly assembled robot hardware capabilities when plugged in.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essential question in robotics is how you connect intelligence to the realities of physical work. A robot has to deal with variation, recover from mistakes, and be useful in environments that weren’t designed around it.

What makes a partner approach valuable is that it brings those realities into the development process. Partners can help identify which tasks matter, what successful performance looks like, and where a system breaks down. That creates a feedback loop between building the technology and learning from its use.

So, to me, the value isn’t simply having more partners. It’s whether those relationships help answer the hard questions: Can the robot generalize? Can it operate reliably? And does it actually make someone’s work easier?

r001.rationale: The response says partners can inform task priorities and system failures, but it does not identify commercially deploying companies or explain collaboration as an indirect way for Pi to advance its research frontier.
